summary:
Aragón stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 on real and effective equality for trans persons and the guarantee of LGBTI rights applies uniformly across the country's autonomous communities, and no Aragón-specific deviation from that position has been identified. A visitor to Aragón is therefore governed by the national rules on recognition, discrimination and sentencing.

Under Article 43 of the law, any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution. It replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment, and no prior surgical reassignment is required. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination: the gender marker recorded in the civil registry, not biological sex, is the operative basis for facility rules. A visitor whose documents have been rectified presents the marker obtained through that administrative route.

Discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics are defined and sanctioned, discriminatory contract clauses are declared null and void, and LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing is addressed. Protections for unmarried same-sex couples are strengthened by the same statute.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months. Both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so an attack motivated by gender expression has no free-standing offence and must be charged through the general offences, with the transphobia aggravation applied at sentencing.

Courts are applying that aggravation. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used it for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, with two minors judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005.
tangentialFactors:
Spain is recognised in comparative international rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries, and Human Rights Watch described the February 2023 passage of the national law as a victory in the fight for gender recognition. Comparative standing of this kind describes the general climate rather than any guarantee in a specific encounter.

The recognition provisions for children from age 12 proved politically contentious during the law's passage, which indicates sustained parliamentary and public debate over the statute a visitor is relying on, though the provisions are in force.

The two documented applications of the transphobia aggravation both arose in other autonomous communities rather than in Aragón, so they establish that Spanish courts use the tool, not that Aragón courts have done so.
localsOnly:
Residents may rectify the gender mention on their own registry entry before the Civil Registry from age 16 without diagnosis, treatment or surgery, and recognition is available from age 12 under conditions; consent rules for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16 are set by the same law.

Employers, service providers and public bodies must collect discrimination data broken down by the causes the law covers, and measures adapted to rural circumstances are mandated — a provision of particular weight in Aragón, where much of the territory is sparsely populated.

Discriminatory contract clauses are null and void, and discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics are sanctionable administrative and civil wrongs, alongside the criminal provisions.

Same-sex couples may marry and adopt on equal terms, and the law strengthens the position of unmarried same-sex couples.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source any Aragón-specific implementing measure: whether the Gobierno de Aragón maintains its own regional LGTBI or trans statute, a regional hate-crime protocol, or a designated pathway for registry rectifications through the Aragón health service is unresolved here.

No figures are available for the number of gender-marker rectifications processed in Aragón, the processing time actually observed at Aragón Civil Registry offices, or any refusal or appeal recorded there.

Whether an Aragón court has applied the Article 22.4 transphobia aggravation is not sourced; the two documented applications are from Vigo and Valencia.

Entry and visa screening practice, including any treatment of gender markers on third-country passports at Spanish border points, is not covered by the source inventory.

Enforcement data on the Article 510 hate-speech provision and on discrimination complaints brought under Ley 4/2023 is not sourced beyond the two case reports.
